description.narrative:
Overall, the POWER programme, has contributed to a more inclusive, and increasingly intersectional womens movement has emerged. By strengthening its partners both institutionally and programmatically KtK has made it possible them to engage in multiple networks, partner with other donors and engage in collective advocacy. The programme has had an impact on Womens rights organisations (WROs), women leaders, community members (including men), and duty bearers. It has made tangible gains in political representation, GBV response, SRHR awareness, economic participation, and grassroots mobilization, despite systemic and contextual challenges.
Objective 1: Strengthening the Women's Movement Key Results: Institutional Strengthening: All 10 longterm and 1 shortterm partner improved planning, monitoring, and financial systems. Nine partners showed marked improvement in PMEL and RBM. Partners like RWGRF and S4S achieved strong financial compliance. Human Rights-Based Approach (HRBA): Applied in community dialogues, advocacy, and tools like ORWOCHs DV Law Scorecard. Increased community accountability. Intersectionality: Movement includes rural women, PLHIV, persons with disabilities, and LBTQ groups. Networking and Advocacy: Over 150 women from all 15 counties convened in a national consultative conference. The outcome of the conference was a jointly developed Womenifesto, which was presented to the President of Liberia.
Objective 2: Political Participation and Peacebuilding Key Results: Women's Leadership: 40 rural women assumed leadership roles at least 6 ran for national office. LIWENs radio campaign reached 6,000 people, leading to increased public support for women leaders. Policy Advocacy: Increased womens representation in government (e.g. 39% of ministers, 40% of all appointments). Peacebuilding: Traditional and local mechanisms were used (e.g. peace huts, community mediation committees). Conflict resolution efforts reached over 2,400 individuals. Attitude Shift: Male support for womens leadership increased, as shown in media engagements and focus groups.
Objective 3: GBV Protection & SRHR Access Key Results: Service Delivery: 412 survivors received case management, counselling, and referrals. Community paralegals enhanced legal documentation. Prevention Efforts: Peer educators, girls clubs, and paralegal training improved SRHR knowledge and reduced GBV stigma. Legal Reform & Accountability: ORWOCH and others contributed to CEDAW reporting and national advocacy on antiFGM and safe abortion laws. ORWOCH also developed a DV Law Scorecard and trained ToTs on DV Law. Community Impact: There was a 30% increase in formal GBV complaints (per HCL). Men and traditional leaders showed increased support for reporting and survivor protection.
Objective 4: Womens Economic Empowerment (WEE) Key Results: Skills and Income: Over 400 women trained in small business skills, smart agriculture, or recycling. Initiatives included tailoring, soap making, food processing, and plastic-to-product recycling. Inclusion: WEE activities targeted women with disabilities, rural women, and LBTQ women. Support Structures: 4 VSLAs were created mentorship systems were strengthened post training. Linkages: Participants connected to buyers and markets via privatesector partnerships (e.g., EcoPlast and recycling firms). Beneficiaries reported increased financial independence and leadership capacity. Women now generate income, manage savings, and engage in local decision-making. There is also improved integration of WEE with SRHR and political participation.
